content: 1. Umbilical Vein Catheterization The umbilical vein catheterization procedure is typically performed for resuscitation or exchange transfusion in neonates, particularly within the first few days of life. In some cases, it may be feasible up to five days after birth. To insert the catheter, first prepare the umbilical cord by cleaning it and the surrounding skin with an antiseptic solution. Tie a suture around the base of the cord and cut the cord 1–2 cm from the base using a sterile scalpel. Identify the umbilical vein, which is the larger, thin-walled vessel, and distinguish it from the two smaller, thicker-walled umbilical arteries. Hold the cord near the umbilical vein with sterile forceps. Using sterile forceps, advance the catheter into the umbilical vein for a distance of 4–6 cm. Ensure the catheter is not kinked and that blood can be easily aspirated. If there is resistance, gently pull back the catheter and reinsert. Secure the catheter with two sutures into the cord, leaving 5-cm-long suture ends. Tape the sutures and catheter securely. After removal, apply pressure to the umbilical stump for 5–10 minutes. 2. Insertion of a Nasogastric Tube Measure the required length of the nasogastric tube by holding its tip against the child’s nose and measuring the distance from the nose to the earlobe, then to the xiphisternum (epigastrium). Mark the tube at this point. Firmly hold the child and lubricate the tip of the tube with water. Insert the tube into one nostril and advance it slowly into the stomach. The tube should pass easily without resistance. Once the measured distance is reached, secure the tube to the nose with tape. Confirm placement by aspirating stomach contents with a syringe and testing the pH using litmus paper (stomach contents turn blue litmus paper pink). If there is any doubt about the tube’s position, withdraw it and reinsert. Once the tube is correctly placed, attach a 20-ml syringe (without the plunger) to the tube and allow food or fluid to flow by gravity. If oxygen therapy is required simultaneously, pass both tubes through the same nostril or use the mouth for the feeding tube. 3. Lumbar Puncture Contraindications for lumbar puncture include signs of raised intracranial pressure (e.g., unequal pupils, rigid posture, limb paralysis, or irregular breathing) and skin infection at the needle insertion site. If contraindications are present, weigh the risks of the procedure against the potential diagnostic value. In cases of doubt, consider initiating treatment for suspected meningitis and delaying the lumbar puncture. Position the child either lying on their side (for young infants) or sitting upright (for older children). Ensure the vertebral column is parallel to the surface and the back is flexed. An assistant should hold the child firmly, ensuring the airway remains unobstructed. Identify the intervertebral space between the third and fourth or fourth and fifth lumbar vertebrae. Prepare the site using aseptic technique, including scrubbing hands, wearing sterile gloves, and cleaning the skin with an antiseptic solution. Use a lumbar puncture needle with a stylet (22-gauge for young infants, 20-gauge for older children). Insert the needle into the intervertebral space, aiming toward the umbilicus. Advance the needle slowly, applying more pressure to penetrate the ligament and less as the dura is pierced. In young infants, the decrease in resistance may not be felt, so proceed cautiously. Withdraw the stylet to allow cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) to flow. If no CSF is obtained, reinsert the stylet and advance the needle slightly. Collect 5–1 ml of CSF in a sterile container. Afterward, withdraw the needle and stylet completely, apply pressure to the site, and cover it with a sterile dressing. If the needle is inserted too far, a lumbar vein may be punctured, resulting in a traumatic tap with bloody CSF. 4. Insertion of a Chest Drain Pleural effusions should be drained unless they are small. In some cases, both sides of the chest may need to be drained, and repeated drainage may be necessary if fluid reaccumulates. Sedation or light anesthesia with ketamine may be considered. Wash hands, wear sterile gloves, and clean the skin over the chest with an antiseptic solution (e.g., 70% alcohol). Select a point in the mid-axillary line just below the nipple level (fifth intercostal space). Inject 1 ml of 1% lignocaine into the skin and subcutaneous tissue at this point. Insert a needle or catheter through the skin and pleura, aspirating to confirm the presence of pleural fluid. Withdraw a sample for microscopy and other tests. If the fluid is clear (straw-colored or brownish), withdraw enough fluid to relieve distress, then remove the needle or catheter and cover the puncture site with a dressing. If the fluid is thin pus or cloudy, leave the catheter in place for repeated drainage, ensuring the catheter is sealed to prevent air entry. For thick pus that cannot pass through the needle or catheter, insert a chest tube. To insert a chest tube, make a 2–3 cm skin incision along the intercostal space, just above the rib below. Use sterile forceps to puncture the pleura and clear a path. Insert the drainage catheter (16-gauge) into the chest, ensuring all drainage holes are inside. Connect the catheter to a collection bottle with an underwater seal, secure it with sutures and tape, and apply a gauze dressing. 5. Suprapubic Aspiration Perform suprapubic aspiration only in a child with a full bladder, confirmed by percussion. Do not use urine bags for specimen collection, as they may become contaminated. Under sterile conditions, insert a 23-gauge needle into the midline, just above the pubis, at the proximal transverse crease. Aspirate to a depth of 3 cm to collect urine. 6. Measuring Blood Glucose Blood glucose can be estimated using reagent strips (e.g., Dextrostix®) at the bedside. Place a drop of blood on the strip and wait for the specified time (30 seconds to 1 minute, depending on the brand). Compare the color change on the strip to the scale provided on the box. For more accurate results, some strips can be used with an electronic reading machine. After wiping off the blood, insert the strip into the machine, which provides a precise glucose value. 7. Drug Dosages and Regimens Drug dosages for infants and children are typically calculated based on body weight to minimize errors. Dosages are provided for a range of body weights (3–29 kg). For neonates in the first two months of life, specific dosages are outlined separately. For certain drugs, such as antiretrovirals, exact individual doses should be calculated based on body weight or surface area. Approximate surface area values for different weight categories can be used to verify calculations. This version ensures clarity and precision while maintaining the technical details necessary for medical professionals.
